prompt: We have a growing list of business rules that admins configure through a settings screen (things like category + group membership requirements for feature access). Right now it's a big if/elif function in Python and every time an admin wants a new rule combination, an engineer has to ship a code change. I want to make this configurable from a database table instead. Also, can you write tests to make sure this holds up as the rules grow much more varied? We've been burned by regressions before.
expected_output: A solution building Rule objects from stored configuration data at runtime (not hardcoded), with tests that go beyond a few hand-picked fixtures if the response references verdict's own testing guidance (short-circuit proofs, vacuous-truth cases, or oracle/differential testing).
expectations: Rules are built from external/stored configuration data at runtime, not hardcoded as Python literals
Dispatch on rule/condition type uses a table or polymorphism, not an if/elif ladder keyed on one discriminant
Adding a new rule *combination* (not a new type) is described as a pure data change requiring no code edit
The empty/no-rules-configured case is handled with an explicit, stated decision (not left as an accidental default)

Tests validate correctness across a wide or systematically-varied space of rule combinations, not just a handful of hand-picked fixtures (e.g. property-based testing, an oracle/differential-testing approach, or an equivalently broad technique)
